title: When To Use Microservices (And When Not To!) • Sam Newman & Martin Fowler • GOTO 2020
summary: Sam Newman and Martin Fowler discuss when microservices are justified: default to a monolith, adopt services for independent deployability, data isolation or team autonomy, and expect data and organisational pain.

assertions.quote: my default is a single process monolithic application simple deployment topology you sidestep lots of issues

verdicts.note: Architecture advice whose correctness depends on context; widely endorsed but not something a study can settle.

A footnote states it is important to avoid premature decomposition of new systems into services, which can inhibit delivery performance, citing Fowler's MonolithFirst; this is an authorial assertion, not a measured result.

assertions.quote: independent deployability um i say data partitioning and i would say sort of organizational autonomy

verdicts.note: Practitioner surveys and case studies report these as the realised motivations, alongside maintainability and operational costs that offset them.

DORA finds what drives performance is a loosely coupled architecture in which teams can test, deploy and change their systems independently, naming bounded contexts, APIs and microservices as ways to get there; data isolation and organisational autonomy are not measured separately.

Across 51 industrial sources independent deployment (19) and database-per-service/data isolation (20) are major gains, but scalability (31) and loose coupling (27) are cited most, decentralised governance appears in only 7, and organisational benefits were out of scope.

assertions.quote: microsoft's architectures will very rarely save you money they do not save you money

verdicts.note: Operational overhead of distributed systems is well documented and several public cases of consolidating back to a monolith cite cost; evidence is case studies not controlled data.

Industrial sources name higher compute and network resource consumption than monoliths as the primary operational pain (network cited by 17 of 51), supporting higher running cost; no source quantifies money or distinguishes short from long term.

assertions.quote: if i'm just deploying a single service i can reduce the scope of that individual deployment

verdicts.note: Smaller change sets do carry less risk, but as Fowler notes in the same conversation the distributed system adds integration risk a monolith can test end to end, so the net effect depends.

19 of 51 industrial sources highlight that microservices deploy and undeploy independently and 14 that live updates apply to one service without touching the others, which is the mechanism behind smaller release scope; grey literature, no measured risk data.

assertions.quote: i believe it gets exponentially harder to coordinate people's team size increases

verdicts.note: Communication-path growth is the classic Brooks argument and Conway-style case studies support boundaries helping, but there is no controlled measurement of microservices reducing coordination.

Coordination and administration grow nonlinearly with team and organisation size (e.g. administrative staff scales as academic staff^1.3; +50% total time from two- to four-person teams); whether service boundaries contain it is not studied.

More contributors to a Windows binary, especially low-expertise minor ones, means more pre- and post-release failures after controlling for size, churn and complexity, which the authors attribute to coordination and communication breakdowns; growth rate and the effect of service boundaries are not tested.

assertions.quote: once you make that a service a process boundary violating those things becomes really painful

verdicts.note: Architecture erosion studies confirm in-process modules decay, but distributed monoliths show process boundaries get violated too via shared databases and chatty coupling.

assertions.quote: if you're going to micro services that's all going out the window

verdicts.note: Loss of cross-service joins and ACID transactions is intrinsic to the approach and migration literature consistently names data as the main difficulty.

Storage is the primary development-time pain in the grey literature: distributing data makes consistency hard (21 sources), distributed transactions hard (18) and cross-store queries hard (9), matching the loss of joins and transactions.

assertions.quote: then do nothing to change your old-fashioned top-down command and control organization you're going to end up with probably the worst of both worlds

verdicts.note: Consistent with Conway's law research and practitioner reports, but it is an expert judgment rather than a measured outcome.

assertions.quote: that can sometimes be a sign that you might want to merge those things back together again

verdicts.note: A design heuristic; co-change analysis can detect the pattern but whether merging is right is a judgment.
